newsitem.title: USA: Clinton-Hashimoto to discuss dlr/yen--Fed's Rivlin.
newsitem.headline: Clinton-Hashimoto to discuss dlr/yen--Fed's Rivlin.

text.p: Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said she expected President Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to talk about the dollar and the yen at their meeting on Friday afternoon.

"I'm sure they (Clinton and Hashimoto)'ll talk about it, they'll talk about the dollar and yen. I don't know what they'll say," Rivlin said in an interview aired late Thursday on the television channel Fox News's Cavuto Business Report program.
Asked if she thought the dollar was too strong, Rivilin said, "I don't comment on the dollar."
But Rivlin said the strong dollar has been a positive factor to contain U.S. inflation.

"We had a strong dollar for some time and on the inflation front, the dollar has certainly been healthy," Rivlin told Fox News. "One of the reasons why we did not have more inflation, given the fact that the economy is growing so fast, is that the dollar has been strong, imports have been cheap."
Rivlin also gave a positive assessment of the U.S. economy, with inflation as the only foreseeable danger at the moment.

"The reassuring thing about this economy is that it has been growing so evenly across industries and across regions," Rivlin said. "We really don't have soft spots in the economy at the moment. The question is can we keep it going... We just have to worry whether it is growing too fast."
Rivlin explained the Fed had to think "about not what is happening now but what might be happening six months to a year from now" when it tightened credit on March 25.
Rivlin declined to predict whether the Fed will raise short-term rates again or by how much.

"What the Federal Reserve, the Open Market Committee did a couple of weeks ago was to say we are concerned about the economy growing too fast in the future, we raised the federal funds rate a quarter point," Rivlin said. "Is that enough? I can't tell yet."

"Wages have been going up, that's clear, prices have not yet. We have to see how rapidly wages are going up, how fast the economy is growing, and make a judgment about what might be happening a year from now," the Fed vice chair also said.
Rivlin stressed "the concern at the Federal Reserve is how do we keep this good growth going and if the economy is growing too fast, then we will have inflation and it will impair the growth."
Commenting on "wonderful growth in jobs," Rivlin said "Nobody wants to close that down."
She noted the higher-than-expected labor force growth rate which may account for stronger growth without inflation.
"We have also been lucky with the labor force growing. So that helps, it relieves some of the pressure," Rivlin added.
The vice chair also agreed the Consumer Price Index likely overstates inflation, though possibly by a smaller margin than some experts estimate.

"What most economists think is that the CPI overstates inflation to some extent... Nobody is sure exactly how much. "I don't know exactly how much it overstates it either," Rivlin admitted. "Nobody wants to underestimate inflation... We should also take a very conservative estimate of how much it may be overstated."
